state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you explain why you think changing all values by the same proportion wouldn't affect the range? What happens to the differences between the heights of the plants when they are cut in half or grow by the same amount?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I thought that if you cut all the heights in half, the differences between them would stay the same, so the range wouldn't change. But now I'm not sure if that's right. When you grow them by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \), does that change the differences too? Can you help me understand how the range works with those changes?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: You're on the right track in recognizing that changing the values by the same proportion can affect the differences between them. Can you think of a specific example with numbers to see how cutting the heights in half or growing them by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) might change the range?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher effectively engages the misconception and maintains cognitive demand through questioning, but makes a mathematical error in Turn 3 by suggesting proportion changes 'can affect' differences (when halving actually does change the range), and the student shows confusion rather than clear progress by Turn 2.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses probing questions to guide the student's thinking and never directly provides the answer, though they could have more explicitly used a counterexample to expose the flawed reasoning about proportional changes.
